'''Theodore Samuel Motzkin''' ({{Langx|he|תיאודור מוצקין}}; 26 March 1908 – 15 December 1970) was an [[Israel]]i-[[United States|American]] [[mathematician]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Motzkin | first=Theodore S. | title=Theodore S. Motzkin: Selected papers |editor=David Cantor |editor2=Basil Gordon |editor2-link=Basil Gordon |editor3=Bruce Rothschild | series=Contemporary Mathematicians|publisher=Birkhäuser | location=Boston, Mass. | year=1983 | pages=xxvi+530 | isbn=3-7643-3087-2 | mr=693096 |author-link=Theodore Motzkin}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Motzkin's father [[Leo Motzkin]], a [[Ukrainian Jews|Ukrainian Jew]], went to [[Berlin]] at the age of thirteen to study mathematics. He pursued university studies in the topic and was accepted as a graduate student by [[Leopold Kronecker]], but left the field to work for the [[Zionism|Zionist]] movement before finishing a dissertation.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Motzkin|mode=cs1}}</ref>

Motzkin grew up in Berlin and started studying mathematics at an early age as well, entering university when he was only 15.<ref name="mactutor"/> He received his [[Ph.D.]] in 1934 from the [[University of Basel]] under the supervision of [[Alexander Ostrowski]]<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=46034}}</ref> for a thesis on the subject of [[linear programming]]<ref name="mactutor"/> (''Beiträge zur Theorie der linearen Ungleichungen'', "Contributions to the Theory of Linear Inequalities", 1936<ref name="debio">{{cite encyclopedia |author=Joachim Schwermer |author-link=Joachim Schwermer |title=Motzkin, Theodor Samuel |encyclopedia=Neue Deutsche Biographie |volume=18 |year=1997 |pages=231 ff |url=http://www.deutsche-biographie.de/pnd119439182.html}}</ref>).

In 1935, Motzkin was appointed to the [[Hebrew University]] in [[Jerusalem]], contributing to the development of [[mathematical terminology]] in [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]].<ref name="debio"/> In 1936 he was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Oslo.<ref>{{cite book|author=Motzkin, Th.|chapter=Sur le produit des spaces métriques|title=In: Congrès International des Mathématiciens|pages=137–138|year=1936}}</ref> During [[World War II]], he worked as a [[cryptographer]] for the British government.<ref name="mactutor"/>

Motzkin married Naomi Orenstein in Jerusalem. They had three sons there.<ref name="mactutor"/>

In 1948, Motzkin moved to the United States. After two years at [[Harvard University|Harvard]] and [[Boston College]], he was appointed at [[UCLA]] in 1950, becoming a professor in 1960.<ref name="debio"/> He worked there until his retirement.<ref name="mactutor"/>

== Contributions to mathematics ==
Motzkin's dissertation contained an important contribution to the nascent theory of linear programming (LP), but its importance was only recognized after an English translation appeared in 1951. He would continue to play an important role in the development of LP while at UCLA.<ref name="debio"/> Apart from this, Motzkin published about diverse problems in [[algebra]], [[graph theory]], [[approximation theory]], [[combinatorics]], [[numerical analysis]], [[algebraic geometry]] and [[number theory]].<ref name="debio"/>

The [[Motzkin transposition theorem]], [[Motzkin number]]s, [[Motzkin–Taussky theorem]] and the [[Fourier–Motzkin elimination]] are named after him. He first developed the "double description" algorithm of [[polyhedral combinatorics]] and [[computational geometry]].<ref>
{{ cite book |last1=Motzkin|first1=T. S.|last2=Raiffa|first2=H.|author-link2=Howard Raiffa|author-link3=Gerald L. Thompson|last3=Thompson|first3=G. L.|last4=Thrall|first4=R. M.|author-link4=Robert M. Thrall|chapter=The double description method| title=Contributions to the theory of games|issue=28 |pages=51–73| series=Annals of Mathematics Studies|publisher=Princeton University Press|location=Princeton, N. J.|year=1953|volume=2 |mr=60202}}</ref> He was the first to prove the existence of [[principal ideal domain]]s that are not [[Euclidean domain]]s, <math display=inline>\mathbb{Z}\left[\frac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}\right]</math> being his first example.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Motzkin |first=Th |date=December 1949 |title=The Euclidean algorithm |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society/volume-55/issue-12/The-Euclidean-algorithm/bams/1183514381.full |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=55 |issue=12 |pages=1142–1146 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1949-09344-8 |issn=0002-9904|doi-access=free }}</ref>

{{Anchor|Motzkin polynomial}}He found the first explicit example of a [[Positive polynomial|nonnegative polynomial]] which is not a [[Polynomial SOS|sum of squares]], known as the Motzkin polynomial {{nowrap|<math>X^4Y^2+X^2Y^4-3X^2Y^2+1</math>,}} and showed that it was positive using the [[AM–GM inequality#Motzkin|AM–GM inequality]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Motzkin | first = T. S. | contribution = The arithmetic-geometric inequality | location = New York | mr = 0223521 | pages = 205–224 | publisher = Academic Press | title = Inequalities (Proc. Sympos. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, 1965) | year = 1967}}</ref>

The quote "complete disorder is impossible," describing [[Ramsey theory]], is attributed to him.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Complete Disorder is Impossible: The Mathematical Work of Walter Deuber | author = Hans Jürgen Prömel | journal = [[Combinatorics, Probability and Computing]] | year = 2005 | volume = 14 | pages = 3–16 | publisher = Cambridge University Press | doi = 10.1017/S0963548304006674 | s2cid = 37243306 }}</ref>
